`require()` loads a module synchronously. Inside a function, that work happens in the middle of the first call instead of at startup, and a missing module throws only when that call is made. The file's dependencies are also no longer listed in one place.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```js
function readConfig(path) {
  const fs = require("fs");
  return fs.readFileSync(path, "utf8");
}
```

{/* bad */}
```js
if (process.env.TRACE) {
  require("./trace");
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
const fs = require("fs");
const { join } = require("path");
const logger = process.env.TRACE ? require("./trace") : require("./quiet");

function readConfig(path) {
  return fs.readFileSync(join(path, "config.json"), "utf8");
}
```

A function of your own that is named `require` is not reported:

{/* good */}
```js
function load(require) {
  return require("settings");
}
```

## When not to use it

Loading a heavy module only when it is needed makes startup faster, and an optional dependency has to be required inside `try`. If you do either often, leave this rule off.
